Project

Editorial approach

Knowing the evidence, recognising the limits and respecting human diversity.

Templates by content type

Biographies, concepts, schools, experiments, everyday articles, clinical dossiers and instruments each have their own structure.

What they all share

Authorship · Review where appropriate · Date · References · Related content · A channel for reporting errors.

History and evidence kept apart

An idea's historical importance and its current scientific support are explained separately.

Experiments in context

Classic studies include their period, ethics and later revisions. Historical cases are not presented as enough evidence to generalise.

No diagnosis at a distance

We avoid retrospective diagnoses of famous people and do not turn traits into labels.

Diversity

We deliberately include women researchers, non-Western contexts and psychology's links with social history.

Careful bilingualism

We keep term equivalences and review translations. An article can be translated; a test also needs its linguistic and cultural version validated.

Nothing empty presented as complete

What is in preparation is labelled as such. The home page shows what is available.

Network

Links with other sites

We link when it meets a reader's need; each article is complete on its home site.

Sources for the structure: Psychology curricula at UNED and UAM (our own organisation inspired by their subjects), the APA's classification of fields, International Test Commission guidelines and the WHO's description of mental disorders.
